Unlike most Milgram studies, where the focus is on levels of obedience (which we ourselves did measure through number of shocks administered), our primary interest lies in levels of concern for the Learner while people obey (and, in this regard, the higher levels of obedience in VR paradigms are an advantage for our purposes). We measured concern through (a) helping behaviour (i.e. the extent to which the correct answer on each trial was pronounced louder than the other three—incorrect—answers); (b) the delay between receiving an incorrect answer and administering a shock, and; (c) self-assessed somatic arousal (indicating stress).

decisions.reason: Under the Codebook relationship rule, this study is not_a_replication because it collects new data (N=40 experimental, N=20 control) using a modified Virtual Reality adaptation of Milgram's proximity paradigm and Slater et al. (2006) as an experimental task to test novel empirical hypotheses (H1: vocal emphasis helping vs. no-Learner control; H2a/H2b: primed science identification moderating helping, shock delay, and dAPQ somatic arousal), rather than re-testing a specific published empirical finding from Milgram (1963) or Slater et al. (2006). Milgram's 65% baseline obedience finding and 1974 'agentic state' theoretical explanation are cited as background motivation and theoretical target, while earlier film/archival observations of participant tension and vocal cueing (Milgram 1965/1974; Millard 2014) are explicitly described as anecdotal observations for which this study provides the first systematic experimental test. Although the authors record completed trials/withdrawals (6/40) and note Slater et al.'s (2006) unprimed, unprodded VR withdrawal count (6/23), they explicitly state obedience is 'not a response variable of interest in the current research' and exclude it from their statistical models and hypothesis tests, using the VR paradigm's high obedience rate instrumentally to observe behaviour while obeying.
